title: Interval-Level Counting Functions
content: primesInLevel(l) counts primes in the l-th primorial interval I(l) = (l!, (l+1)!], and qualifyingInLevel(l) counts those additionally satisfying AFSC (all factorial subtractions composite). These are defined via Finset.filter on PrimorialInterval from OQ-02. The key bound q(l) ≤ p(l) (every qualifying prime is a prime) is proved by Finset.card_le_card applied to the subset relationship between the two filtered sets.
mathContext: $p(l) = |\{n \in (l!, (l+1)!] : n \text{ prime}\}|$, $q(l) = |\{n \in (l!, (l+1)!] : n \text{ prime} \wedge \text{AFSC}(n)\}|$. By definition, $q(l) \leq p(l)$ since qualifying primes form a subset of primes.

title: The Strong Selberg Density Axiom
content: The strong axiom states q(l)·(l+1) ≥ p(l)·l for l ≥ 3, meaning the qualifying fraction q(l)/p(l) is at least l/(l+1). This is motivated by the Selberg sieve: each of the l+1 'bad' conditions (p - k! composite for some k ≤ l) eliminates at most O(l!/log²(l!)) primes by Brun-Titchmarsh, while the total is ≈ l!/log(l!) by PNT, so the bad fraction is O((l+1)/log(l!)) → 0. The axiom captures the leading behavior with the clean threshold l/(l+1). The companion axiom primes_growth_in_levels (p(l) ≥ l for l ≥ 3) is an extremely weak consequence of PNT — the actual count is astronomically larger.
mathContext: Axiom: $q(l) \cdot (l+1) \geq p(l) \cdot l$ for $l \geq 3$, equivalently $\frac{q(l)}{p(l)} \geq \frac{l}{l+1}$. From Brun-Titchmarsh: non-qualifying primes in $I(l)$ are $\leq (l+1) \cdot \frac{2 \cdot l!}{\log^2(l!)}$, while $p(l) \approx \frac{l!}{\log(l!)}$, giving bad fraction $\leq \frac{2(l+1)}{\log(l!)} \to 0$.

title: Strong Axiom Recovers the Weak Selberg Axiom
content: strong_implies_weak proves that the strong axiom gives q(l) ≥ 1 for l ≥ 3, recovering the weak selberg_density_axiom (at least one qualifying prime per interval). The chain: from the axioms, q(l)·(l+1) ≥ p(l)·l ≥ l² ≥ 9 > 0, so q(l) ≥ 1. From q(l) ≥ 1, extract a specific element via Finset.card_ne_zero → Finset.Nonempty → ∃ element. This confirms the strong axiom strictly generalizes the weak one.
mathContext: $q(l)(l+1) \geq p(l) \cdot l \geq l^2 \geq 9 > 0 \implies q(l) \geq 1$. The extraction $q(l) \geq 1 \implies \exists p \in I(l), \text{Prime}(p) \wedge \text{AFSC}(p)$ uses the correspondence between cardinality $\geq 1$ and nonemptiness.

title: Level-Wise Density Bounds and Strict Surplus
content: Two key results: levelwise_density_bound proves q(l)·(k+1) ≥ p(l)·k for l ≥ k (the qualifying fraction at level l exceeds any threshold k/(k+1) as long as l ≥ k). The proof splits q·(l+1) = q·(k+1) + q·(l-k), uses q ≤ p to show q·(l-k) ≤ p·(l-k), and combines with the axiom. levelwise_strict_surplus proves a ≥1 unit surplus for l ≥ max(3, k+2). It uses equality analysis: if q·(k+1) = p·k (no surplus), then q·(l+1) = p·l forces q·(l-k) = p·(l-k), but cross-multiplying gives p·(l-k) ≤ 0, contradicting p ≥ l ≥ k+2 > 0.
mathContext: For $l \geq k$: $q(l)(k+1) \geq p(l) \cdot k$, i.e., density $\frac{q(l)}{p(l)} \geq \frac{k}{k+1}$. For $l \geq k+2$: $q(l)(k+1) \geq p(l) \cdot k + 1$ (strict surplus). The surplus comes from the gap between $\frac{l}{l+1}$ and $\frac{k}{k+1}$ when $l > k$.

title: Main Theorem: Density at Factorial Evaluation Points
content: density_at_levels is the main result: for every threshold k, there exists N such that for all n ≥ N, the cumulative sum ∑_{l=3}^{n} q(l)·(k+1) ≥ ∑_{l=3}^{n} p(l)·k. The proof technique is surplus accumulation: split the sum at a cutoff L₀ = max(3, k+2). For l ≥ L₀, each level contributes ≥1 unit of surplus (from levelwise_strict_surplus). The early levels l < L₀ contribute a finite deficit D (bounded by a constant depending only on k). For n ≥ L₀ + D, the accumulated surplus n - L₀ + 1 > D exceeds the deficit.
mathContext: For all $k$, $\exists N$: for $n \geq N$, $\sum_{l=3}^{n} q(l)(k+1) \geq \sum_{l=3}^{n} p(l) \cdot k$. At factorial evaluation points $x = (n+1)!$, this gives $\frac{C(x)}{\pi(x)} \geq \frac{k}{k+1}$ for all $k$, hence density $\to 1$.

title: Gap Analysis: Why General x Remains Open
content: A detailed analysis explains why the density result cannot be extended from factorial points to general x without additional ingredients. Between x = n! and x = (n+1)!, the interval (n!, (n+1)!] has size n · n! — growing factorially. The partial-interval deficit (primes counted but not yet known to be qualifying) can be as large as p(l) · k, growing factorially. But the cumulative surplus from prior levels grows only linearly in the number of levels. Three possible approaches are identified: (a) within-interval sieve estimates, (b) monotonicity of C(x)/π(x), (c) a direct cumulative density argument.
mathContext: At $x = n! + t$ for $0 < t < n \cdot n!$: deficit from partial interval $\leq p(n) \cdot k \approx \frac{n!}{\log(n!)} \cdot k$, but cumulative surplus from levels $3, \ldots, n-1$ is $\leq n - L_0$. Since $\frac{n!}{\log(n!)} \gg n$, the surplus cannot absorb the deficit.
